Subject: Connectivity options for our regulated pilot

Hi Irene,

Thanks again for the product overview yesterday. We're starting a small regulated pilot (PII, logs retained 7 years, audited) and need to choose a connectivity model for Redwood Private. High level constraints:

- No public internet egress for inference traffic; must stay within our cloud accounts or a direct link.
- Auditability: must capture flow logs and be able to hand them to security for SOC-like review.
- Low single-digit 10s ms RTT from app to model for our 512-token workloads in us-east-1.
- Minimal ops: security team prefers managed endpoints over DIY tunnels where feasible.
- Cross-account: Redwood will be in a different AWS account than our inference VPCs.
- Budget: we prefer predictable monthly cost; data transfer variability is a concern.

Attached is a short network requirements doc (HarborNetworkRequirements.pdf).

Could you outline the tradeoffs for: VPC peering, PrivateLink (interface endpoints), and site-to-site IPsec VPN? Specifically: feasibility with cross-account, monitoring/auditability, expected latency/throughput, and any operational caveats.

Best,
Sam

Sam — thanks for the clear requirements and the PDF. Looping in Karthik (solutions) and Monica (acct lead). I'm sticking a concise option matrix in the attachments (connectivity-option-matrix.xlsx) and below outline recommended tradeoffs for your security team to review.

Short summary up-front: none of the three is a perfect one-size-fits-all. For a regulated pilot with auditability and low latency priorities, an interface-endpoint (PrivateLink) based control plane + either VPC peering or a managed IPsec (for encrypted customer-controlled tunnels) for bulk data are common hybrid patterns. That said, if you want minimal ops and fully managed AWS-native approach, interface endpoints to a PrivateLink service are attractive — but they come with per-endpoint IP management and throughput considerations.

High-level bullets (full details in Karthik's note below):
- VPC peering: lowest added latency, straightforward routing, but not transitive (you need route management across accounts and regions); good for high-throughput but control plane exposure must be evaluated.
- PrivateLink (interface endpoints): best for cross-account least-privilege access and avoids route table changes; easier to restrict ports; per-endpoint interface ENIs mean additional monitoring surface and some per-GB charges.
- Site-to-site IPsec VPN: encrypts over public internet (unless you use Direct Connect), predictable monthly cost if static, can be managed by your side — but usually higher latency and extra ops for key rotation and tunnel failover tuning.

Next steps proposal: 1) Karthik to sketch the detailed operational tradeoffs (routing examples, flow-log placement, monitoring hooks). 2) We run a short PoC (3–5 days) with PrivateLink control-plane + peering for hot path, measuring p95 latency and egress accounting. 3) Procurement: Monica to start a procurement note in HS-12345 for estimated monthly costs.

Thanks —

Thanks @Irene — adding a more technical view so Harbor's infra and security folks can vet. I tried to provide concrete examples and actionable warnings rather than a vendor-sell.

1) VPC peering (cross-account):
- Routing: AWS VPC peering is simple L3 routing between VPCs; you add routes in each VPC's route table for the peer CIDRs. No NAT or proxy required.
- Transitivity: not supported — you must peer each pair. For multi-VPC architectures this can be cumbersome.
- Latency: minimal (single-digit ms within same AZ/region typically). Good for low-latency inference.
- Security/audit: Flow logs can be enabled per VPC (VPC Flow Logs -> CloudWatch/ S3) in your account. Because traffic is cross-account, you'll want logging in your account and an ingestion pipeline for Redwood logs for correlation.
- Ops: You must manage route updates and potential overlapping CIDR blocks. Works well when you control the VPC address plan.
- Cost: No data transfer charges for inbound/outbound within same AZ; cross-AZ/regional transfers may incur charges.

2) PrivateLink / Interface endpoints (Redwood exposes a PrivateLink service):
- Mechanism: Redwood deploys a Network Load Balancer fronting internal service; you create Interface Endpoints in your VPC which create ENIs with private IPs and route via AWS' private networking. This is cross-account friendly.
- Isolation: Very useful for least-privilege (you only open specific ports to the endpoint). No route table edits needed beyond security groups.
- Latency & throughput: Latency is low but slightly higher than peering due to the ENI/NLB hop — expect a few ms overhead. Throughput per ENI is good for typical inference traffic; if you have bursty very-high throughput, you may need multiple endpoints or scale-up patterns.
- Auditability: Flow logs capture ENI-level traffic; because endpoints live in your account, you can centralize logs. PrivateLink also makes it easy to limit egress to only specific services.
- Cost: Per-hour + per-GB data charges for endpoints. Predictability is reasonable but per-GB charges add variable cost.
- Ops: Easier for cross-account because Redwood can publish the service name and you simply create the endpoint. Key caveat: interface ENIs show up in your VPC which you must include in your asset inventory and monitoring.

3) Site-to-site IPsec VPN (managed by you or a managed partner):
- Mechanism: Standard IPsec tunnels over the internet or via Direct Connect/Transit Gateway.
- Latency: Higher and more variable than AWS-native options; internet-based tunnels subject to public internet variability.
- Security & compliance: Strong encryption in transit; however, auditability for connection health and flow logs is less direct — you'd need packet/flow capture at your edge or on instances and store logs to meet audit needs.
- Ops: Key rotation, MTU tuning (DF issues), and BGP/route flapping handling can be non-trivial. Managed VPN appliances or AWS VPN can reduce ops but still require runbook work.
- Cost: Usually a predictable monthly charge for managed VPN + data egress costs.

4) Hybrid patterns & recommendations for a regulated pilot:
- Option A (managed-minimal ops): PrivateLink-only for control + data for small pilots. Pros: least privilege, simple cross-account setup, easy to audit ENI flows. Cons: extra per-GB costs, you need to design for ENI scaling.
- Option B (latency-first): VPC peering for data plane inside a shared region + PrivateLink for control plane/API calls. Pros: lowest latency for data; cons: requires CIDR planning and route management.
- Option C (customer-controlled encryption): IPsec (optionally over Direct Connect) when customers insist on managing their own perimeter and full control over keying.

Operational notes for Harbor's security team:
- Flow logs: enable at ENI and VPC level; export to your S3 audit bucket with retention rules.
- Tracing: add request-id propagation in the SDK calls so model call latency can be correlated with network-level logs.
- Monitoring: expose endpoint health via CloudWatch metrics and forward to your security SIEM.
- PoC baseline: measure p95 token latency on the 512-token workload, CPU/GPU utilization on Redwood side, and data transfer costs for a week of simulated traffic.

Attaching a simple E2E flow diagram (plank_e2e_flow.drawio) that shows where flow logs and ENIs live and a short option matrix (connectivity-option-matrix.xlsx).

Irene / Monica — happy to run the PoC and provide a short runbook for whichever path Harbor picks.
